metadata.title: Claude, Expansion Kickoff.
metadata.subtitle: What a Skill Actually Is
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Plain register: did Claude learn how to run an expansion when it picked up the expansion-kickoff skill? Lands the carry-out that a skill is a file of steps Claude reads before it starts, not new model knowledge.
metadata.anchor_pair: B03 -> B06 (expansion-kickoff's single SKILL.md: planted, then returned to)

beats.narration_text: Call something the expansion-kickoff skill and it sounds like a capability Claude picked up. It didn't. Underneath, it's one file of instructions Claude reads before it acts. Let's take it apart.

What is a skill?

beats.narration_text: Hear "Claude has an expansion-kickoff skill" and the mind fills in a strategy upgrade — like Claude studied business expansions and came back knowing something it didn't before. That's the natural read of the word 'skill'.

Nothing in the model changes. Delete the folder and Claude doesn't forget how to plan an expansion — there was nothing there to learn. It just stops running that one routine. That tells you where the skill actually lives: outside the model.

Here's what a skill actually is: one file. Expansion-kickoff is a folder holding a single SKILL.md — instructions for starting a structured checklist when a team or business expands somewhere new, written in plain language Claude reads before it acts. The file is the program.
Claude reads that file top to bottom and works each step in the order written. No branching, unless a step in the file explicitly says branch. Linear — on purpose.

That makes a skill a specification, not a new capability. What they optimized for: the same checklist, every kickoff — repeatable starting steps, every time. What that costs: anything the file didn't write down, Claude is off the map.

So expansion-kickoff never taught Claude how to run a real expansion. It guarantees that every time it runs, Claude reads that same file and starts the same structured checklist. That's the whole trick — a design choice made honest.

beats.narration_text: Watching Claude produce a tidy kickoff plan doesn't prove it understood the business — a checklist can be followed to the letter on a situation it never really grasped. And a rough plan doesn't prove the skill is broken — it may just be a case the file's steps don't fit. Neither result is proof.
A skill doesn't teach Claude how to run an expansion. It's a file of steps Claude reads before it starts, so every kickoff runs off the same checklist — the same starting steps, every time.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: pick one process I repeat every time I start something new. Write me a SKILL.md for it — plain language, ordered steps — then read it back, and walk me through exactly what you'll do, before you do it. Go deeper: which step would you cut, and what does keeping it actually buy?

llm_exercise.prompt: Pick one process I repeat every time I start something new — a research kickoff, a client onboarding, a code review, whatever. Write me a SKILL.md for it: a title, one paragraph on when to trigger it, then plain-language ordered steps I'd want you to follow. Then read the SKILL.md back to me and walk me through exactly what you would do the next time I invoke it, before you do it.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: which step in that SKILL.md would you cut if I made you drop one, and what does keeping it actually buy me that the other steps don't already cover?
